items.headline: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
items.blurb: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.
items.text: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment. The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said. Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days. Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said. The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.

items.headline: Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
items.blurb: Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah.
items.text: Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group. Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA). The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities. “In light of the investigation’s findings, the prime minister ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said. The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said. Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption. items.text: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. items.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
items.blurb: The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments - a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed".
items.text: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties". The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory. items.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
items.blurb: The social media giant is accused of not informing 20 million users it had access to their photos.
items.text: Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent. Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app. It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately. The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant. The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts. Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery. items.blurb: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
items.text: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said. The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways. items.headline: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
items.blurb: SpaceX has performed the historic catch using mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".
items.text: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time. "Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower. But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea. The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

items.headline: ‘Tackling inequality is key for India in age of change’: Economist Joseph E Stiglitz at HT Leadership Summit
items.blurb: He also warned that climate impacts will hit tropical regions hard and said national economic sovereignty may increasingly shape global policy.
items.text: The US in the twilight of its power and China needing to reorient its economy away from exports to domestic consumption are the central contradictions facing today’s global economy, economist and Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz said at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit on Saturday. The new world order will be multipolar unlike the unipolar US-dominated world order that existed after the second world war. Adjusting to it will not be easy for all countries. India’s key opportunity and challenge lies in managing its domestic inequality; and if done well, there is no reason the nation cannot sustain high levels of growth, the US economist said. What the world needs to navigate this phase is the leadership of young, idealistic and pragmatic people. It also needs the rest of the world, especially the so-called middle powers, to stand up together against bully-like behaviour from the US, which is what it has become under President Donald Trump , he added. items.blurb: According to Stiglitz, the ongoing AI boom has generated two key challenges for the global economy: expected returns and balance in the global economy.
items.text: The lack of a macroeconomic model for Artificial Intelligence (AI) makes it a double-edged sword for nations, Nobel Prize winning economist Joseph Stiglitz said at the Hindustan Times Leadership summit on Saturday, while cautioning that countries like India should increase investments in education to mitigate the potential impact it could have on employment. According to Stiglitz, the ongoing AI boom has generated two key challenges for the global economy. The first is whether the investments in AI will lead to expected returns, which in turn would determine if it creates a financial sector bubble that would eventually burst. The second and more important challenge is striking a balance between the gainers and losers which AI will create in the global economy. The resignation of Huang from the company he co-founded in 1993 has divided opinions. They also argued that replacing Huang with someone else could be detrimental to the world’s second-most valuable company. items.headline: How to ensure that AI disruption doesn’t leave workers behind
items.blurb: Policymakers and business leaders have important roles to play in supporting U.S. citizens through the AI transition.
items.text: Jay Clayton, a former U.S. attorney, is now—in the president’s words—America’s “AI czar.” More formally, he is head of the White House’s new Super Intelligence Force. In that role, Clayton is responsible for developing “plans for responding to SI-enabled threats” to America. That remit is a fine starting place for Washington, which, until very recently, been concerningly disengaged with regulating or overseeing the artificial-intelligence industry at all. Attending to concerns around AI threats to privacy, national security, and perhaps even civilization are of critical importance. But there must be just as much attention placed on addressing the more immediate transition into the AI era—things like retraining workers, making sure displaced workers are supported, and ensuring government and private businesses have a way to work together through big economic changes. A failure to meaningfully address these shorter-run, more mundane concerns may mean we never reach the promised AI era at all. items.text: It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. items.headline: ‘Holy Grail of spaceflight’: SpaceX pulls off first-ever midair 'catch' of Starship returning from orbit
items.blurb: SpaceX achieved the first catch of a Starship spacecraft, guiding the 171-foot vehicle into the arms of its launch tower after a 22-hour orbital mission. The ship completed 14 laps around Earth and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, while its booster exploded shortly after liftoff.
items.text: Elon Musk-owned SpaceX on Saturday (local time) pulled off the first-ever ‘catch’ of a spaceship, marking a milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems. SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique. According to Reuters, the 171-foot-tall Starship fell out of thick clouds over SpaceX's Starbase launch site, reignited engines to flip itself vertical, and slowly descended into the tower's "Mechazilla" arms, engines still roaring. Charred from the blazing heat of its return from space, the ship shut down its engines and hung still after the rocket system's longest mission yet. The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 124-meter behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the US-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites. items.headline: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
items.blurb: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
items.text: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago. Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .”

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. items.blurb: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially…
items.text: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. On The Vergecast: The many spiraling stories in the AI world, the fate of streaming services, Mark Zuckerberg’s meat, and more. One part of the saga surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ended on Thursday, when Huang resigned from his position at the top of AI’s most important company. But in the coming weeks and months, a much bigger story may be about to unfold. items.headline: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
items.blurb: New research shows the most advanced AI models from China were trained on banned Nvidia chips.
items.text: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. items.headline: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
items.blurb: LangChain now claims 7,000 customers of its model and platform agnostic agent management tool LangSmith.
items.text: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. items.headline: Jensen Huang’s Exit: How Deep Does NVIDIA’s AI Ecosystem Run In India?
items.blurb: Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the…
items.text: NVIDIA’s influence in India extends far beyond GPU sales, spanning AI infrastructure, software, developer ecosystems, startup incubation and direct equity investments. With Indian data centre operators committing billions of dollars to NVIDIA-powered infrastructure, and enterprises and startups building on its CUDA-led software stack, the company has become deeply embedded in the country's AI ambitions. As Jensen Huang exits, the bigger question is whether India can reduce its dependence on a single technology provider, particularly as geopolitical uncertainties, export restrictions and competing chip architectures reshape access to AI compute. Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions. From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India’s AI industry.
